a: the sanctuary made new again
p: The verb is the one that gave the feast of Dedication its Greek name.
b: The Greek verb is enkainizō, "make new, dedicate". Its noun, enkainia, is the Greek name of the feast that Judas set up when he purified the Temple in 164 BC (4:52–59), and John's Gospel uses it for the winter feast at which Jesus walked in Solomon's porch (John 10:22). The Hebrew name, Hanukkah, also means "dedication". Chapter 5 follows soon after that feast: the rededicated altar is what sets the neighbors against the Jews.

a: the nations on every side
p: The chapter is a tour of the hostile neighbors: Edom, Ammon, Gilead, Galilee, the coast.
b: "The nations" (ta ethnē) in 1 Maccabees are the non-Jewish peoples around Judea. After the Temple was cleansed, Jews living as minorities among them came under attack, and the chapter follows Judas from one front to the next: south against Idumea (5:3–5), east across the Jordan (5:6–8, 24–54), and Simon north to Galilee (5:21–23). The picture recalls Psalm 83, where a ring of nations says, "Come, we will wipe them out so they are no nation" (Psalm 83:4). The writer wants readers to see Judas as the one who answered that old threat.

a: the descendants of Esau
p: The Edomites had moved into southern Judea; their land was now called Idumea.
b: "The sons of Esau" are the Edomites (Genesis 36:1). After Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, Edomites moved north into the hills around Hebron, which then took the Greek name Idumea, "land of Edom" (5:65). Old bitterness against Edom runs through the prophets (Obadiah 1:10–14; Psalm 137:7). The story did not end with Judas: about forty years later John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea and made its people accept circumcision and the law (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258), and from that people came Herod the Great.

a: Akrabattene
p: Two places fit the name, one south of the Dead Sea and one near Shechem.
b: Akrabattene could be the district of the Scorpion Pass, the "Ascent of Akrabbim" on Judah's southern border (Numbers 34:4; Joshua 15:3), which suits a war with Edom. Or it could be the district of Akraba, southeast of Shechem, which Josephus calls Akrabatene. Most commentators prefer the southern site here, because the verse speaks of Idumea (see the variant).

a: a trap and a snare
p: The words Joshua used for the Canaanites Israel failed to drive out.
b: Joshua warned that the nations left in the land "will become a trap and a snare for you" (Joshua 23:13; compare Exodus 23:33). The writer uses the same pair for the sons of Baean, an otherwise unknown tribe that ambushed Jews on the roads. Some link the name with Beon, a town east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:3), but no one knows. The words cast Judas's campaign as unfinished business from the conquest.

a: He put them under the ban
p: Judas does to the sons of Baean what Joshua did to Jericho.
b: The verb anathematizō is the Septuagint's word for the Hebrew cherem, devoting a city to destruction (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:21). In the books of the 66 the ban is commanded for the peoples of Canaan (Deuteronomy 20:16–17). The sons of Baean were not Canaanites, and no prophet commands the ban here; the writer simply reports it, with approval. Here 1 Maccabees goes beyond the 66 books, applying Joshua's war law to a new enemy. Readers who hold the book as Scripture usually read it as an accurate report of what Judas did, not as a command for others; see the deep section on chapter 5.

a: Timothy
p: A commander in Transjordan who fights Judas through this chapter, and in 2 Maccabees.
b: Timothy (Timotheos, a Greek name) leads the Ammonites here and the coalition in Gilead (5:11, 34, 37–44). He was probably a local governor of the Seleucid king. 2 Maccabees tells of a Timothy too (2 Maccabees 8:30–32; 10:24–38; 12:2–25), but its order of events differs, and it seems to have him killed at Gazara (2 Maccabees 10:37) before he fights again in chapter 12. Scholars still debate whether there were two Timothys or one story told two ways.

a: the Israelites who lived in their territory
p: Jewish farmers and towns had spread into Gilead and Galilee long before the revolt.
b: By the 100s BC Jews lived well outside little Judea: in Gilead east of the Jordan, in Galilee, and along the coast. Many in Gilead were tied to the Tobiad family (see 5:13). They were minorities among Greek-speaking and Arab neighbors, and the Maccabean victory put them in danger. Notice what Judas does: he does not annex Gilead or Galilee but brings the Jews home to Judea (5:23, 45). Only later Hasmonean kings conquered these lands.

a: the district of Tobias
p: Either the old land of Tob, or the estates of the Tobiad family east of the Jordan.
b: The Greek says only "in the [places] of Toubias". Two readings are offered. It may be the land of Tob, where Jephthah fled (Judges 11:3), east of the Sea of Galilee. Or it may be the lands of the Tobiads, a powerful Jewish family descended, many think, from "Tobiah the Ammonite" who opposed Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:10). Their estate and fortress at Iraq al-Amir, west of modern Amman, is described by Josephus (Antiquities 12.230–233) and can still be visited. 2 Maccabees 12:17 calls the Jews there "Toubians".

a: Galilee of the foreigners
p: An old name, from Isaiah, for the mixed north.
b: Isaiah spoke of "Galilee of the nations" (Isaiah 9:1), and Matthew quotes the line when Jesus begins to preach there (Matthew 4:15). Here the Greek has allophylōn, "of the foreigners", the word this book uses for non-Jews (and the Septuagint for the Philistines, as in 5:66). In the 160s BC Galilee had Jewish villages among many non-Jewish ones, with the Phoenician cities of Ptolemais (Acco), Tyre and Sidon on its western edge.

a: a great assembly
p: The word ekklēsia, later used for the church, here means Israel gathered to decide.
b: The Greek ekklēsia is the Septuagint's regular word for the Hebrew qahal, the gathered people of Israel (Deuteronomy 31:30). In 1 Maccabees the assembly makes decisions with its leaders (also 3:44; 14:19). The New Testament took the same word for the gathering of Jesus' followers, the church (Matthew 16:18).

a: Simon
t: The three brothers divide the work
p: Simon takes Galilee; Judas and Jonathan take Gilead. All three will lead Israel in turn.
b: This is the first time the book shows the brothers working as a team. Judas leads until his death (9:18), Jonathan after him (9:30), then Simon, who becomes high priest and ruler (13:8; 14:41). The writer's point, made openly in 5:62, is that God chose this family to save Israel.

a: the gate of Ptolemais
p: The port of Acco, refounded by the Ptolemies under a new name.
b: Ptolemais is Acco (Judges 1:31), renamed by Ptolemy II of Egypt in the 200s BC. It was a Greek city and a Seleucid base, and later (12:48) Jonathan would be captured there. Paul stayed a day with believers there (Acts 21:7). On "gate" or "towns", see the variant.

a: He took along the Jews from Galilee and Arbatta
p: The Greek says only "he took them"; the Plain names who they were.
b: The Greek has "he took them along from Galilee and Arbatta". "Them" are the Jews of 5:14–17, so the Plain says so. Arbatta (Greek Arbaktois; ℵ and V spell it otherwise) is unknown; it may be Narbata, near Caesarea, or a district of the coastal plain. Simon brings the Jewish families to Judea, as Judas does in Gilead (5:45).
orig: παρέλαβεν αὐτοὺς (parelaben autous), 'he took them along'

a: the Nabateans
p: The Arab kingdom of Petra greets Judas in peace.
b: The Nabateans were Arab traders whose capital was Petra in Edom's old land. Their king is the Aretas of 2 Maccabees 5:8, and a later Aretas controlled Damascus when Paul escaped it (2 Corinthians 11:32). Here they meet Judas "in peace" and pass on news of the Jews in Gilead. Not every Arab group was friendly: in 9:35–36 the sons of Jambri kill John, Judas's brother.

a: Carnaim
p: Some can be placed: Bozrah is Bostra, Carnaim is the old Ashteroth-karnaim.
b: Bozrah (Bossora) is probably Bostra (Busra al-Sham), not the Edomite Bozrah of Isaiah 63:1. Carnaim is the ancient Ashteroth-karnaim, "Astarte of the two horns", where Chedorlaomer struck the Rephaim (Genesis 14:5). Bosor, Alema, Chaspho and Maked are less certain; scholars place them in the Hauran and the Golan, east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee.

a: killed every male with the edge of the sword
p: Judas's treatment of hostile towns follows Deuteronomy's law of war for distant cities.
b: Deuteronomy tells Israel to offer peace to a distant city, and if it refuses, "strike down every male in it with the sword" (Deuteronomy 20:13), while sparing women and children. The book reports the same sentence at Bosor, Maapha and Ephron (5:28, 35, 51), and at Ephron it first has Judas offer peace (5:48), just as Deuteronomy 20:10 says, "offer it peace". So it presents him as keeping the law of war. Modern readers ask whether that law can be kept at all; whether Christians may fight is carded at Deuteronomy 20, and the deep section on this chapter takes it further.

a: the cry of the town was going up to heaven
p: The phrase echoes the Philistine town struck by God in 1 Samuel 5.
b: The Greek reads like the Septuagint of 1 Samuel 5:12, where "the town's cry for help rose up to the sky". In both, a town in distress cries out; here the cry comes from the besieged Jews, and Judas is its answer. Heaven is also this book's reverent word for God (3:18, 50; 4:10), so "up to heaven" may mean "up to God".

a: He sounded the trumpets, and they cried out in prayer
p: The war trumpet in the law is a way of calling on God.
b: The law told Israel: "sound the battle blast on the trumpets. Then the LORD your God will remember you, and you will be rescued from your enemies" (Numbers 10:9). Judas sounds the trumpets and his men pray at once. (Alexandrinus says "he" sounded them; Sinaiticus and Venetus say "they".) The book never names God in these chapters, but the prayer shows whom they trust (compare 3:54; 4:13, 40).

a: Maapha
p: The town's name is uncertain; many think it is Alema of 5:26.
b: The town Judas takes after the rescue is Maapha in Alexandrinus and Mapha in Sinaiticus; the Latin and the KJV have Maspha, that is Mizpah of Gilead (Judges 11:29). Because 5:36 lists the other towns of 5:26 but not Alema, many scholars think this is Alema, and the name was spoiled in copying. The Plain keeps the Greek.

a: If he crosses over to us first
p: Timothy reads the first move as a sign, like Jonathan son of Saul at Michmash.
b: Timothy decides that whoever crosses the stream first will win. That is a known kind of battle omen. Saul's son Jonathan made a similar test at Michmash: if the Philistines said "Come on up to us," then "The LORD has handed them over to us" (1 Samuel 14:10). Here the enemy sets the sign, and Judas, by crossing first (5:43), unknowingly fulfills it against him.

a: the officials of the people
p: The Greek grammateis are the officers of Deuteronomy 20, who sent men home from battle.
b: The Greek is grammateis, usually "scribes". But in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew shoterim, "officials", the officers who in Deuteronomy 20:5–9 tell the army who may go home before battle. In 3:55–56 Judas did just that. Here he gives them the opposite order: let no one stay in camp. The site renders shoterim "officials", so the Plain does the same here.

a: the sacred precinct at Carnaim
p: Carnaim's temple belonged to the Syrian goddess Atargatis, according to 2 Maccabees.
b: A temenos is the walled holy ground around a temple. 2 Maccabees 12:26 says that Judas struck at Carnaim and "the Atargateion", the temple of Atargatis, the great Syrian goddess. Temples were places of refuge in the Greek world, and the enemy flees there for safety. Judas burns it with those inside (5:44), as Jonathan later burns the temple of Dagon at Azotus (10:84).

a: burned the precinct with fire, with everyone in it
t: Burning a temple full of refugees
p: The book tells it as victory; many readers since find it hard to read.
b: The enemy had thrown down its weapons (5:43). To the writer, burning a pagan shrine and those in it is zeal for God, like Josiah burning the shrines of Bethel (2 Kings 23:15–16) and Deuteronomy's command to burn the nations' sacred objects (Deuteronomy 12:3). Christian moral teaching has judged acts of war differently: the Catechism names the deliberate killing of the defenseless as a crime even in a just war (Catechism 2313–2314), and many Jewish readers too have treated these campaigns as history, not as a pattern. Whether Christians may fight at all is carded at Deuteronomy 20.

a: This large town guarded the way in
p: The town blocked the only road home; on its wording see the variant.
b: Ephron is probably et-Taiyibeh, near Irbid in northern Jordan, on the road down to the Jordan valley opposite Beth-shan. 2 Maccabees 12:27 tells the same story. The Greek of Alexandrinus calls it the town "of the entrance", the gateway into the pass; Sinaiticus and Venetus say it was "on the road".

a: I will go through your land to reach our own land
p: Judas asks for passage in the words Moses used to Edom and to Sihon.
b: Moses asked Sihon, "Let me pass through your land" (Numbers 21:22), and Edom with the same words (Numbers 20:17; compare Deuteronomy 2:27–28, "Just let me pass through on foot"). Both refused, and Sihon came out to fight and was destroyed (Numbers 21:23–24). Judas's message follows that pattern, and it also obeys Deuteronomy 20:10: "When you come near a city to fight against it, offer it peace." Ephron's refusal leads, as in Sihon's case, to its destruction (5:50–51).

a: tore the town up by its roots
p: The verb pictures a city pulled up like a plant.
b: The verb exerizōsen means "he rooted out". It is a prophetic picture: God "uproots" kingdoms (Jeremiah 1:10; compare Zephaniah 2:4, where Ekron is uprooted). Walking "over the bodies of the dead" may mean through streets full of corpses; the writer does not soften it.

a: Beth-shan
p: The city where Saul's body hung was spared, because its Jews spoke for it.
b: Beth-shan, where the Philistines "fastened" Saul's corpse "to the wall" (1 Samuel 31:10), was by now the Greek city of Scythopolis. 2 Maccabees 12:29–31 says that Judas did not attack it, because the Jews living there told him how well its people had treated them. The two accounts together show that Judas's wars were aimed at those who attacked Jews, not at every Greek city.

a: for not one of them had fallen
p: A whole nation on the road, and none lost: a sign of God's care.
b: After the war with Midian the officers reported, "not one man of ours is missing" (Numbers 31:49), and brought an offering. Judas's people go up to Zion and offer burnt offerings for the same reason. The march home with women and children across the Jordan (5:45–53) is told like a small exodus, ending at the sanctuary just made new (5:1).

a: We too should win a name for ourselves
p: The builders of Babel wanted the same thing, and failed.
b: The words recall the tower builders: "We will win a name for ourselves" (Genesis 11:4). In 1 Maccabees an honored name is a real good: Eleazar gives his life "to save his people and gain an everlasting name" (6:44), and Judas's name is praised (3:7; 5:63). But a name taken for oneself, against orders, ends in disaster (5:60). The difference, for this writer, is whether God has chosen you to save Israel (5:62).

a: They were not of the seed of those men by whose hand Israel was given salvation
p: The plainest statement of the book's belief that God saved Israel through the Hasmoneans.
b: This verse gives the moral of 5:55–64. Joseph and Azariah were brave but not chosen; salvation came only "by the hand" of Mattathias's sons. Most scholars read it as the heart of the book's purpose: to show that the Hasmonean family, who became Judea's high priests and later kings, ruled by God's choice (compare 13:3–6; 14:25–49). 2 Maccabees, by contrast, credits the martyrs and God's direct help, and has nothing like this verse. Catholic and Orthodox readers, who hold the book as Scripture, read it as true of that moment in Israel's history, as God once raised up judges.
orig: οἷς ἐδόθη σωτηρία Ἰσραὴλ διὰ χειρὸς αὐτῶν

a: the man Judas
p: A Hebrew way of speaking that puts Judas beside Moses.
b: "The man Judas" (ho anēr Ioudas) is unusual Greek. It copies a Hebrew style used of Moses: "The man Moses was also held in high honor in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 11:3; compare Numbers 12:3). Like Moses, Judas is honored by his own people and feared by the nations. Phrases like this are one reason scholars think 1 Maccabees was first written in Hebrew.

a: He struck Hebron and its villages
p: Abraham's town had been Edomite for centuries.
b: Hebron, where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were buried and where David first reigned (Genesis 23:19; 2 Samuel 2:1–4), lay inside Idumea by this time. The book describes its capture without any comment on its sacred past, which shows how far south the Edomites had come. "Villages" is literally "daughters", a Hebrew way of naming the small towns that belong to a city.

a: passed through Samaria
p: All the Greek manuscripts say Samaria, but the road from Hebron to Philistia runs through Marisa.
b: Samaria lies far to the north, off the route from Hebron to the Philistine coast. Josephus, retelling this verse, says Marisa (Antiquities 12.353), the Idumean town on the way (2 Maccabees 12:35). Many scholars think the Hebrew had "Marisa" (Mareshah, Joshua 15:44) and that an early copyist changed it to the better-known name. Swete's manuscripts, the Latin and the KJV all have Samaria, so the Plain keeps it.

a: That day some priests fell in battle
p: A second warning about brave men acting on their own. 2 Maccabees has a related story.
b: Like Joseph and Azariah (5:61), the priests wanted to win glory, and went out "without thinking it through". The book is a priestly family's history, yet it names this failure. 2 Maccabees 12:32–45 tells of soldiers who fell after a battle with Gorgias, and of what Judas did for them; it belongs to the pages on 2 Maccabees. On the Greek of this verse, see the variant.

a: He tore down their altars, burned the carved images of their gods
p: Judas does what Deuteronomy commanded for the nations' shrines.
b: Deuteronomy said: "pull down their altars, break their standing stones to pieces, chop down their Asherah poles and burn their carved images" (Deuteronomy 7:5; compare Deuteronomy 12:3). Judas does it at Azotus (Sinaiticus adds "with fire"), the old Philistine Ashdod, where Dagon fell before the ark (1 Samuel 5:1–5). The law spoke of the shrines inside the promised land, and Azotus lay within the land's ideal borders (Joshua 15:46–47). Here the book agrees with the 66 books' own pattern of reform (2 Kings 23).

a: the upper provinces
p: In 165 BC Antiochus marched east to raise money, leaving Lysias to deal with Judea.
b: "The upper provinces" are the lands east of the Euphrates: Babylonia, Media, Persia. Antiochus set out in 165 BC, short of money, to collect tribute (3:31, 37). That is why Lysias, his deputy, fought Judas (4:26–35). Polybius, a Greek historian of the same century, confirms that he tried to rob a rich temple in Elymais, failed, and died soon after at Tabae in Persia (Histories 31.9).

a: in Elymais, in Persia, there was a city
t: Elymais: a land, not a city
p: Elymais is the old land of Elam; the Latin and the KJV make it a city's name.
b: Elymais was a region, ancient Elam (Genesis 14:1; Daniel 8:2), at the head of the Persian Gulf. Alexandrinus says "in Elymais in Persia there is a city", which is correct. Sinaiticus and Venetus read "in Lymais", and the KJV and the Latin make Elymais the city itself (see the variant). The temple was that of a goddess the Greeks called Artemis (Polybius) and 2 Maccabees calls Nanea (2 Maccabees 1:13–16). His father, Antiochus III, had been killed in 187 BC trying to plunder a temple of Bel in the same land.
orig: ἐν Ἐλύμαις ἐν τῇ Περσίδι πόλις

a: left there by Alexander son of Philip
p: A legend that tied the temple's treasure to the world's great conqueror.
b: No other source says that Alexander the Great left armor in Elymais. The detail links the end of Antiochus with the book's opening (1:1–7): the empire that began with Alexander is now ruled by a king who cannot even take a temple. Alexander's titles here repeat 1:1.

a: the armies that had marched into the land of Judah had been routed
p: The report sums up chapters 3–5: Lysias beaten, the altar cleansed, the walls rebuilt.
b: The messenger's report runs through 6:5–7 in reported speech. It reviews the defeats of Gorgias and Nicanor (3:38–4:25) and of Lysias (4:28–35), the cleansing of the altar (4:42–47) and the new walls (4:60–61). The book thus makes Judea, not Elymais, the true cause of the king's collapse.

a: the abomination that he had built on the altar
p: The "abomination of desolation" of 1:54 and Daniel, now gone.
b: In 1:54 the king's men set up "an abomination of desolation" on the altar, the phrase of Daniel 11:31 and 12:11, probably a pagan altar or sacred stone. Jesus used the phrase for a future sacrilege (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14). Its removal (4:43–47) is what Antiochus now hears. Readers of Daniel could see Daniel 8:14 come true: "then the holy place will be put right".

a: his town Beth-zur
p: The Greek says "his town": the king's fortress, or a slip for "its town".
b: The Greek polin autou means "his city". It may mean that Beth-zur, the fortress on Judea's southern border (4:29, 61), had been a royal stronghold and was now in Jewish hands. Or "his" may point back to the sanctuary, its guard town. The KJV has "his city Bethsura". Beth-zur is the site of Khirbet et-Tubeiqa, near Hebron, where Hellenistic coins and walls have been dug up.

a: fell sick from grief
p: 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees and Polybius tell Antiochus's death in three different ways.
b: Here Antiochus dies of grief and illness in Persia, confessing what he did in Jerusalem (6:12–13). 2 Maccabees gives two other accounts: priests kill him in the temple of Nanea (2 Maccabees 1:13–16), or God strikes him with worms in his bowels as he races to destroy Jerusalem, and he vows to become a Jew (2 Maccabees 9). Polybius says he went mad, which some ancient writers took as punishment for touching the temple (Histories 31.9). All agree that he died far from Judea, soon after robbing or trying to rob a temple, in 164 BC.

a: he reckoned that he was dying
p: Daniel foresees the king's end in the land of Israel; this book places it in Persia.
b: Daniel 11:40–45 foretells that the arrogant king will pitch his tents "between the seas and the beautiful holy mountain" and "come to his end, and no one will help him." Most critical scholars read Daniel 11 as written during the persecution, accurate up to about 165 BC (11:21–39), with verses 40–45 a prediction that did not happen as written, since Antiochus died in Persia. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers answer that 11:36–45 looks past Antiochus to a final enemy: so Jerome, following the church before him (Commentary on Daniel on 11:21–45). The question is carded on this chapter page.

a: Sleep has left my eyes
p: Like Darius and Ahasuerus, a troubled king cannot sleep.
b: Sleepless kings mark turning points in the stories of the Hebrew Bible: Darius worrying over Daniel (Daniel 6:18), and Ahasuerus, when "That night sleep ran away from the king" (Esther 6:1). Here the night of worry leads not to rescue but to a confession. Antiochus speaks to his court "Friends", the highest rank at a Hellenistic court.

a: into what great waves
p: The Greek klydōn is the surf of a stormy sea.
b: Klydōn is rough water, the surge of a storm (Luke 8:24; James 1:6). The king pictures himself as a man going under, a picture common in the Psalms (Psalm 69:1–2). His claim to have been "good-hearted and well loved" is ironic after chapter 1, where he plundered Jerusalem and burned its books.

a: Now the evil I did in Jerusalem comes back to me
p: The persecutor admits that his suffering is the result of his crimes. Is he sorry?
b: Antiochus confesses three things: the evil done in Jerusalem, the theft of the vessels (1:21–23) and the attack on Judah's people "for nothing". He sees cause and effect, the core of the book's theology of history, but says nothing about God and asks no forgiveness. 2 Maccabees goes further: he vows to free Jerusalem and become a Jew, but the writer says his prayer was not heard (2 Maccabees 9:11–18). Christian preachers often used him as a warning against late repentance driven by fear rather than love.

a: his crown, his robe and his signet ring
p: Crown, robe and ring: the signs of royal power, as in Joseph's and Mordecai's stories.
b: Pharaoh gave Joseph his signet ring and robes (Genesis 41:42); Ahasuerus gave Mordecai the ring he took back from Haman (Esther 8:2). Here the dying king gives Philip the signs of regency over his young son. The choice set up a civil war, since Lysias already had the boy (3:32–33; 6:17, 55–56).

a: in the year 149
p: Year 149 is 164/163 BC. A Babylonian king list puts the news of his death in late 164 BC.
b: 1 Maccabees counts years from the start of the Seleucid kingdom in 312/311 BC, so year 149 is 164/163 BC. A clay tablet from Babylon (BM 35603) records that in month Kislev of year 148, by the Babylonian count (November–December 164 BC), news came that Antiochus had died. That is the same month in which Judas cleansed the Temple (4:52). 1 Maccabees tells his death after the cleansing; 2 Maccabees 9–10 tells it before. The two counts of years (the Babylonian from spring 311, a Macedonian one from autumn 312) explain some of the difference.

a: he named him Eupator
p: The boy king's title honors the father this book calls a sinful root.
b: Eupatōr means "of a good father". Antiochus V was about nine. The title is an irony for the book's readers, who were told in 1:10 that his father was "a sinful root". The boy reigned for under two years and was killed by Demetrius's soldiers (7:2–4).

a: The men in the Citadel
p: The Seleucid fortress beside the Temple held out for about twenty-five years.
b: The Citadel (Greek Akra) was built in 167 BC in the City of David (1:33–36) and held a royal garrison and Jews loyal to the king. From it they could overlook the Temple courts, "hemming Israel in". Judas could not take it; only Simon did, in 141 BC (13:49–52). Its exact site, south of the Temple Mount, is still debated; in 2015 Israeli archaeologists announced remains of a fortification in the City of David that they identified with it.

a: some ungodly men from Israel joined them
p: The war was also a civil war inside Judea.
b: The book calls the Jewish supporters of the king "ungodly" and "lawless" (1:11; 7:5). They had their own case: they had obeyed the government (6:23), and the Maccabees had killed some of them and seized their land (6:24). The revolt was not only Jews against Greeks but also a fight over what it meant to be faithful, a fight that runs through chapters 6–9.

a: our family lands were plundered
p: The Greek says "our inheritances", the family land every Israelite was meant to keep.
b: Klēronomiai renders the Hebrew nachalah, the inherited family land that the law protected (Numbers 27:7–11; 1 Kings 21:3). The complaint is that the rebels were taking land from families who sided with the king. For that, both sides claimed the law's support.

a: thirty-two elephants trained for war
p: The peace of 188 BC forbade the Seleucids to keep war elephants.
b: After Rome beat Antiochus III (8:6), the treaty of Apamea (188 BC) required the Seleucids to give up their elephants (Polybius, book 21; Livy 38.38). Lysias kept or rebuilt a herd anyway. In 162 BC a Roman envoy, Gnaeus Octavius, had the elephants hamstrung and was murdered at Laodicea for it (Polybius, book 31; Appian, Syrian Wars 46). The numbers of men in 6:30 (100,000 foot, 20,000 horse) are far above what the kingdom could field; modern historians such as Bar-Kochva think the real army was much smaller.

a: the blood of grapes and mulberries
p: A Hebrew idiom for red juice or wine, used to rouse the elephants.
b: "The blood of grapes" is an old idiom for wine: Judah washes "his robe in the blood of grapes" (Genesis 49:11), and Israel "drank the blood of the grape, red wine" (Deuteronomy 32:14). The Greek says they "showed" it to the elephants. That may mean the red color was meant to excite them, or that they were given it to drink; 3 Maccabees 5:2 has elephants made wild with wine and frankincense.

a: thirty-two warriors who fought from it
p: No elephant could carry that many; the number is probably an early slip.
b: A war elephant's tower held two to four soldiers. "Thirty-two" may have been copied from the number of elephants in 6:30, or a Hebrew "two" or "three" was misread. Alexandrinus has it, and so does Venetus, as "men of strength, two and thirty", which the KJV follows ("two and thirty strong men"). Sinaiticus has "men of strength and thirty", without "two" (see the variant). The Plain keeps Alexandrinus. The "Indian" is the driver (mahout); trainers from India came with the elephants.

a: stirring up the enemy and closing in among the phalanxes
p: The Greek participles are hard: the horsemen harass, or are shielded, or both.
b: The Greek says the horsemen were kataseiontes kai kataphrassomenoi en tais phalanxin, "shaking (or waving) and fencing themselves in among the phalanxes". The first verb can mean "making signals" (so the KJV, "giving them signs") or "stirring up, harassing". The second can mean "being armored" or "being protected". The Plain keeps both verbs close to their plain sense; whether the horsemen shelter behind the infantry or close up its flanks is not clear.

a: blazed like torches of fire
p: The description makes the enemy dazzling, so that Israel's courage stands out.
b: The writer piles up the army's splendor: gold shields, mountains blazing, the sound of marching and weapons (6:39–41). This is a set piece meant to make the reader afraid, so that Eleazar's charge (6:43–46) shines brighter. Compare the terrifying armies of Joel 2:3–5 and Nahum 2:3–4.

a: Eleazar Avaran
p: The fourth son of Mattathias, named in 2:5; the Greek of Alexandrinus spells his name Savaran.
b: Eleazar was one of Mattathias's five sons (2:2–5), the first of the brothers to die. His surname, Auran in Sinaiticus (and in Josephus, Antiquities 12.373), Auaran in Venetus, has been explained from Hebrew roots meaning "pierce" or "pale"; no one is sure. Alexandrinus writes ho Sauaran, the Latin "son of Saura" (see the variant). He is not the old scribe Eleazar who died for the law in 2 Maccabees 6:18–31.

a: He gave himself to save his people and gain an everlasting name for himself
p: Eleazar chose certain death. The book praises it; later readers asked what kind of death it was.
b: The Greek edōken heauton, "he gave himself", is the language of self-sacrifice. Eleazar did not seek death for its own sake: he aimed to kill the king and save his people, and death was the price. Ambrose held him up as a model of courage (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40.207). Augustine, who taught that taking one's own life is never allowed except by God's special command, as with Samson (City of God 1.21, 1.26), wrote about killing oneself, not about a soldier's deadly risk in battle, and Christian moralists have generally kept the two apart. Josephus tells it twice: the Antiquities says he died after courageously killing many of the enemy (12.373–374), but the Jewish War remarks that he only attempted great things and showed that he preferred glory to life (Jewish War 1.42–44). Compare 2 Maccabees 14:37–46, where Razis kills himself rather than be captured. See the deep section on this chapter.
orig: καὶ ἔδωκεν ἑαυτὸν τοῦ σῶσαι τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ

a: set himself beneath it
p: The Greek says only that he "placed under" it; he probably stabbed it from below.
b: The verb hypethēken means "he placed under". The Latin takes it as "he put himself under it" (supposuit se ei), and the KJV as "thrust him under". Ambrose, retelling the scene, says he slipped under the beast and struck it (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40.207). The belly was the elephant's soft spot. The Plain leaves the Greek's own vagueness.
orig: ὑπέθηκεν αὐτῷ; Latin supposuit se ei

a: they turned away from them
p: The book admits that Judas lost at Beth-zechariah.
b: "They turned away" is a polite way to say Judas's army retreated. For a writer so devoted to the family, the admission matters: the book does not hide defeats (also 5:60; 9:6–18). 2 Maccabees 13:15–22 tells the campaign as a Jewish success. Josephus follows 1 Maccabees (Antiquities 12.375).

a: for it was a Sabbath year for the land
p: Judea was keeping the law's seventh year, and the fields lay unsown.
b: The law says, "in the seventh year the land is to have a Sabbath of complete rest" (Leviticus 25:4; compare Exodus 23:10–11). The Jews kept it even during the war, and so their stores ran out (6:53–54). Josephus also mentions sabbatical years in this period (Antiquities 13.234). The verse is one of the fixed points scholars use to work out the cycle of sabbatical years: 164/163 BC on the most common count.

a: those who had escaped to Judea from the nations
p: The families Judas brought home in chapter 5 now share the little food there is.
b: The rescues of 5:23 and 5:45 filled Judea with refugees. In a Sabbath year, with no harvest, the food in the Temple stores ("in the holy place") ran out. So the victories of chapter 5 led to hunger in chapter 6, and the writer says so plainly.

a: Let us grant that they may walk by their own laws, as before
p: The aim of the revolt is won: the decree of 1:41–50 is undone.
b: Lysias proposes to let the Jews "walk by their own laws", reversing the king's order to abandon them (1:41–50). 2 Maccabees 11:22–26 preserves a letter of Antiochus V that does just this and returns the Temple. From here on, the struggle changes: the question is no longer whether Jews may keep the law, but who will rule them. That is why the Hasideans make peace in 7:13.

a: He broke the oath he had sworn
p: A theme of chapters 6–7: the Seleucid side cannot be trusted.
b: The king swears (6:61) and breaks it at once. In chapter 7 Bacchides and Alcimus offer peace "with treachery" (7:10), Alcimus swears and kills sixty men (7:15–16), and Nicanor tries to seize Judas (7:27–30). The people's verdict comes in 7:18: "There is no truth or justice in them." The theme prepares for chapter 8, where Judas looks for a partner who keeps faith (8:12, 28).

a: took the city by force
p: Philip loses; but a greater rival is about to arrive from Rome.
b: Antioch on the Orontes was the Seleucid capital. Lysias took it back from Philip in 163 or 162 BC. His victory lasted only months: in 162 BC Demetrius escaped from Rome and both Lysias and the boy king were killed (7:1–4).

a: Demetrius son of Seleucus left Rome
p: Demetrius had been a hostage in Rome; the historian Polybius helped him slip away in 162 BC.
b: Demetrius I was the son of Seleucus IV and the rightful heir when his uncle Antiochus IV took the throne. He had been sent to Rome as a hostage, as Antiochus himself once was (1:10). When the Senate refused to let him go, he escaped by ship in 162 BC with the help of friends, among them Polybius, who tells the story himself (Histories 31.11–15). The "town on the coast" is Tripolis in Phoenicia, according to 2 Maccabees 14:1.

a: In the year 151
p: Year 151 of the Seleucid era is 162/161 BC.
b: By the book's count from 312/311 BC, year 151 runs from 162 to 161 BC. Demetrius reached Syria in the autumn of 162 BC. The battle with Nicanor (7:43) followed in the spring of 161 BC, and the treaty with Rome (8:17–32) in the same year.

a: Do not show me their faces
p: Demetrius orders the killing without ordering it.
b: The new king does not want to see his cousin, the boy king Antiochus V, or his regent Lysias. The soldiers understand and kill them (7:4). The book tells it in a few words, as one more turn in the bloody family politics of the Seleucids that the writer had watched for decades (compare 10:50; 11:17).

a: Alcimus, who wanted to serve as priest
p: A priest of Aaron's line, but not of the old high-priestly house, who wanted the high priesthood.
b: Alcimus is a Greek name ("strong"); his Hebrew name was probably Yakim or Eliakim. Josephus says he was of Aaron's line but not of the family of the former high priests (Antiquities 20.235). 2 Maccabees 14:3 says he had already held the office and had "defiled himself". The Greek here says only that he wanted "to be priest" (hierateuein); 7:9 and 7:21 show that the high priesthood was meant. A rabbinic story tells of Yakim of Tseroroth, a nephew of the sage Yose ben Yoezer, who mocked his uncle on the way to execution (Genesis Rabbah 65:22); many scholars identify him with Alcimus.

a: the lawless and ungodly men of Israel
p: The book never lets the Jewish supporters of the kings speak for themselves.
b: "Lawless" (anomoi) and "ungodly" (asebeis) are the writer's names for Jews who sided with the Seleucids (also 3:5–6; 9:23). Their own view was that they were loyal subjects, at peace with the government, and that the Maccabees were rebels who had taken their land (6:23–24; 7:6–7). The book tells only one side, in the language of the Psalms, where "the wicked" oppose "the righteous".

a: who governed the province Beyond the River
p: The old Persian name for the lands west of the Euphrates.
b: "Beyond the River" (Aramaic avar nahara) was the Persian name for Syria and Palestine, used in Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 4:10–11; Nehemiah 2:7). Bacchides governed this region for Demetrius. He will be Judas's last enemy: in 9:1–18 his army kills Judas at Elasa.

a: they set Alcimus up in the priesthood
t: A high priest named by a foreign king
p: Since Jason, the Seleucid kings had sold or granted the high priesthood.
b: In the law the high priesthood passed by descent from Aaron (Numbers 25:10–13). Under the Seleucids it became a royal appointment: Jason bought it from Antiochus IV, and Menelaus outbid him (2 Maccabees 4:7–10, 23–26). Now Demetrius makes Alcimus high priest, with an army to enforce it. Later the Hasmoneans, too, would receive the office from a Seleucid king (10:18–21), and then from the people (14:41).

a: A group of scribes
p: Experts in the law, acting as a body, ready to negotiate.
b: Scribes were the teachers and interpreters of the law, like Ezra, "a scribe, an expert in Moses' law" (Ezra 7:6), and like the scholar praised by Sirach (Sirach 38:24–39:11). Here they come as a group to Alcimus and Bacchides "to ask for fair terms" (dikaia, "just things"). With freedom to keep the law restored (6:59), they saw no reason to fight a priest of Aaron's line.

a: The Hasideans
p: From Hebrew chasidim, "the loyal ones", a group devoted to the law.
b: Asidaioi renders the Hebrew chasidim, "the loyal" or "devout", from chesed, "loyal love". The book first names them in 2:42 as "mighty warriors of Israel" who joined Mattathias. Their being "the first ... to seek peace" shows that their aim was the law, not Hasmonean rule. Who they were is debated: many scholars see them as forerunners of the Pharisees or the Essenes; others think the word was only a description. 2 Maccabees 14:6 has Alcimus call Judas their leader.

a: A priest of the line of Aaron has come with the army
p: The Hasideans trusted Alcimus's descent; the book shows that birth did not make him faithful.
b: The Hasideans reasoned from the law: a son of Aaron would not harm them. The writer, who believes that God chose Mattathias's priestly family (5:62), shows the mistake bloodily (7:16). The point cuts both ways in the book: a right pedigree is not enough, and God's choice is shown by deeds. Scholars who read the book as Hasmonean apology note that it gives the Hasmoneans themselves no Aaronic pedigree beyond Joarib (2:1).

a: as in the words that he wrote
p: "He" is the psalmist; the next verse quotes Psalm 79.
b: The Greek says only "according to the words that he wrote", without naming the writer. A corrector of Sinaiticus added "the prophet" (see the variant), and the Latin has "according to the word that is written". The quotation is from Psalm 79, a psalm of Asaph. The book here treats a psalm as prophecy fulfilled in its own day, the way Matthew does with "so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled" (Matthew 2:17–18; 13:35).

a: The flesh of your loyal ones and their blood
p: The psalm's "loyal ones" are chasidim: the very name of the men just killed.
b: The verse quotes Psalm 79:2–3 in shortened form: "the flesh of your loyal ones" and "Their blood they spilled like water / on every side of Jerusalem, / and there was nobody to bury them". The Greek hosiōn renders the Hebrew chasidekha, "your loyal ones", the same word as "Hasideans" (7:13). So the writer saw the psalm's lament for slaughtered chasidim fulfilled in Alcimus's killing of the Hasideans. Psalm 79 mourns the defiled Temple and the dead; its prayer for God's fury on the nations is carded at Psalm 79.
orig: Σάρκας ὁσίων σου καὶ αἵματα αὐτῶν

a: They have broken the agreement and the oath they swore
p: The Greek stasis here means a standing arrangement; the KJV calls it a covenant.
b: Stasis usually means "position" or "revolt", but here it is a fixed arrangement, an agreement that stands. The KJV renders "the covenant" and the Douay "the covenant", from the Latin constitutum. Breaking an oath made in God's name was, for Jewish readers, a sin against God himself (Leviticus 19:12; Ezekiel 17:15–19).

a: He slaughtered them
p: The verb is the word for killing a sacrificial victim.
b: The Greek ethysen normally means "sacrificed" or "slaughtered (an animal)". The writer may mean only "butchered", but the choice is pointed: the friends of the pagan king "sacrifice" Jews. The bodies thrown into "the great pit" (a well or cistern) recall Ishmael son of Nethaniah, who killed pilgrims and threw them into a cistern at Mizpah (Jeremiah 41:4–9).

a: the men who had deserted to him
p: The Greek can mean men who had come over to Bacchides, or men who had left him.
b: The phrase tōn met' autou automolēsantōn andrōn is unclear. It may mean Jews who had gone over to Bacchides' side and whom he then distrusted; or men "who had deserted with him". The Latin and the KJV take it as men who had fled from him ("that had forsaken him"). The Plain follows the most natural Greek sense, "deserters to him", and leaves the reason for their killing open, as the text does.

a: Alcimus fought hard for the high priesthood
p: Alcimus had the title but not the people.
b: The verb ēgōnisato is "he struggled, contended", as in an athletic contest. Alcimus held the office, backed by an army, but many Jews refused him. He remained high priest until his death in 159 BC, struck down while tearing down a wall of the Temple court (9:54–56).

a: took vengeance on the men, and on those who had deserted
p: Judas punishes the Jews who went over to Alcimus.
b: The war inside Judea grows harsher on both sides: Bacchides kills deserters and Hasideans (7:16–19), and Judas takes vengeance on those who joined Alcimus. The writer approves, as he approved Mattathias's killing of the Jew who sacrificed at Modein (2:24–26). Readers of the book have long noted that it tells a civil war in which both sides killed fellow Jews.

a: Nicanor
p: A royal commander who "hated Israel"; 2 Maccabees tells his story at greater length.
b: Nicanor is called "one of his honored commanders". 2 Maccabees 14:12 calls him the commander of the elephants, and tells that he first became Judas's friend before the king ordered him to seize Judas (2 Maccabees 14:18–30). 1 Maccabees tells it shortly: his peace was treachery from the start (7:27–30). It is probably not the Nicanor of 3:38.

a: Capharsalama
p: "Village of peace", a fitting name for a battle after a false peace.
b: Capharsalama means "village of peace" (Hebrew kefar shalom). Its place is uncertain, perhaps near Gibeon northwest of Jerusalem. Alexandrinus writes the name oddly (Charpharsarama); the Plain gives the form of Sinaiticus' corrector, Venetus and the Latin (see the variant).

a: they fled to the City of David
p: Probably Nicanor's men, who took refuge in the Citadel, which stood in the City of David.
b: The Greek says only "and they fled". Since the Citadel stood in the City of David (1:33), and Nicanor next appears on Mount Zion (7:33), most take it that the survivors of Nicanor's army fled there. Josephus, however, says that Nicanor beat Judas and that Judas fled to the citadel in Jerusalem (Antiquities 12.405), which is strange, since the Citadel was the king's. Most commentators keep the book's account, in which Nicanor's men fall and flee. The number of the fallen also differs (see the variant).

a: the burnt offering being offered for the king
p: The Temple offered sacrifice for the ruling king, a custom from Persian times to AD 66.
b: The priests show Nicanor that Jerusalem is loyal: they offer sacrifices for the king. Darius had asked the Jews to "pray for the life of the king and of his sons" (Ezra 6:10), and Jeremiah had told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7). Josephus says that daily sacrifices for the Roman emperor were offered until AD 66, when stopping them began the war with Rome (Jewish War 2.409). Paul likewise asks for prayers for kings (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

a: He defiled them
p: He made the priests unclean, perhaps by spitting or by touching them.
b: Emianen means "he defiled". Priests on duty had to stay ritually pure (Leviticus 22:1–9), and an insult such as spitting would make them unclean and unable to serve (compare Numbers 12:14). The Douay has "abused them". The book lists his mockery, defilement and arrogance as blasphemy, which is why the priests' prayer asks God to remember it (7:38).

a: You chose this house, for your name to be called over it
t: The house called by God's name
p: The priests pray in the words of Solomon's dedication prayer.
b: The prayer echoes Solomon: "they will know that your name has been called over this house I built" (1 Kings 8:43; compare 1 Kings 8:29). "A house of prayer" recalls Isaiah 56:7, which Jesus quoted when he cleared the Temple (Mark 11:17). As everywhere in these chapters, God is not named: the priests say only "you". The book uses "Heaven" or simply "you" for God, out of reverence (3:18–19; 4:10).
orig: ἐπικληθῆναι τὸ ὄνομά σου ἐπ᾽ αὐτόν

a: Remember their blasphemies
p: A plea from the laments over the ruined Temple.
b: Psalm 74, a lament for the burned sanctuary, prays: "Remember this, LORD: the enemy jeers" (Psalm 74:18), and "Remember the insults a fool throws at you all day" (Psalm 74:22). The priests ask the same. The plea is answered: the man who stretched out his hand against the Temple loses that hand (7:47).

a: your angel went out and struck down a hundred eighty-five thousand of them
p: Judas recalls the night God saved Jerusalem from Assyria.
b: The prayer points to 2 Kings 19:35: "The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria: one hundred eighty-five thousand" (compare Isaiah 37:36). Sennacherib's men had mocked Israel's God (2 Kings 19:22), as Nicanor had (7:34–35, 42). Judas does not name the Assyrian king or God; the KJV and the Latin add a name (see the variant). 2 Maccabees 15:22 has Judas pray with the same example.

a: on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar
p: March 161 BC, the day before Purim.
b: Adar is the twelfth month, in late winter. The thirteenth of Adar is the day in Esther on which the Jews' enemies had planned to destroy them and were themselves destroyed, with Purim kept on the fourteenth and fifteenth (Esther 9:1, 17–19). 2 Maccabees 15:36 makes the link: Nicanor's Day is "the day before Mordecai's day". For the book's readers, a second deliverance had fallen on the same date.

a: outflanked them
p: The Greek pictures horns closing around the enemy.
b: The verb hyperekerōn comes from keras, "horn", the word for the wing of an army. The villagers swept round the fleeing army's wings and drove it back toward Judas's pursuers, so it was caught between them. The Latin keeps the picture: ventilabant eos cornibus, "they tossed them with horns".

a: They cut off Nicanor's head, and the right hand he had stretched out so arrogantly
p: The hand that threatened the Temple is shown to Jerusalem, as Goliath's head once was.
b: Nicanor had stretched out his hand against the Temple (7:35; 2 Maccabees 14:33). Now his head and right hand are hung up near Jerusalem. David "cut off his head" from Goliath and "carried the Philistine's head to Jerusalem" (1 Samuel 17:51, 54), and Judith's people hung Holofernes' head on the wall (Judith 14:1, 11). The Talmud tells the story with the thumbs and big toes cut off and hung at Jerusalem's gates (Bavli Taanit 18b).

a: They resolved to keep this day every year
p: A yearly holiday, still on the Jewish calendar in the first century AD.
b: Nicanor's Day was kept for centuries. Megillat Ta'anit, a first-century list of days on which no one might fast, names the thirteenth of Adar as the day of Nicanor. Both Talmuds tell of it (Bavli Taanit 18b; Yerushalmi Taanit 2:12). Later, the thirteenth of Adar became the Fast of Esther, before Purim, and the holiday was forgotten. The feast is one more sign that the Maccabean victories were built into Jewish worship, as Hanukkah was (4:59).

a: So the land of Judah was quiet for a few days
t: Quiet, but only for a few days
p: The words of Judges, with a sad change: not forty years, but a few days.
b: Judges closes each deliverance with the same words: "So the land was quiet for forty years" (Judges 3:11; compare Judges 3:30; Judges 8:28). The writer tells Judas's story as a book of Judges, with Judas as the judge God raised up. But the rest lasts only "a few days"; in chapter 9 Bacchides returns and Judas falls.

a: Judas heard what the Romans were known for
t: The first Jewish portrait of Rome
p: Warm and admiring: written before Rome conquered Jerusalem, and unlike Daniel 7 or Revelation.
b: Chapter 8 is the earliest Jewish description of Rome that survives, and it is full of praise: strong, loyal to friends, free of kings and envy. The 66 books see Rome very differently. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have taken Daniel's fourth beast, "terrifying and dreadful", as Rome (Daniel 7:7, 23), though critical scholars read it as the Greek kingdoms. Revelation pictures Rome as the beast from the sea and as Babylon, drunk with the blood of God's people (Revelation 13:1–8; 17:5–6, 9). The difference is mostly one of date: 1 Maccabees was written before Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC. On how 1 Maccabees fits with these books, see the deep section on this chapter.

a: they made friends with anyone who joined them or came to them
p: Philia is the Greek for Rome's amicitia, a formal bond between states.
b: Philia, "friendship", is not a feeling here but a diplomatic status: Rome's amicitia. A state that was a "friend and ally" of the Roman people (8:20) was listed as such in Rome. The bond cost Rome little and gave it a reason to interfere when it chose. Alexandrinus repeats a clause here ("whoever joins them"), which Sinaiticus and Venetus lack; the Plain keeps both thoughts in one line.

a: the Gauls
p: The Greek Galatai can mean the Gauls of the west or the Galatians of Asia Minor.
b: Rome fought both: the Gauls of northern Italy, conquered between 225 and 191 BC, and the Galatians of central Asia Minor, defeated by the consul Manlius Vulso in 189 BC (Livy 38.12–27). The Galatians were Gauls who had settled in Asia Minor; Paul later wrote to churches among them (Galatians 1:2). Since "tribute" fits Rome's western conquests better, many take this as the Gauls of Italy and Spain's neighbors; but a Jew in Judea would have heard more of the Galatians.

a: the silver and gold mines there
p: Rome won Spain from Carthage and worked its famous mines.
b: Rome took Spain from Carthage in the war against Hannibal (218–201 BC) and spent the rest of the century fighting the Spanish tribes. The silver mines near New Carthage (Cartagena) were famous; Polybius, as quoted by Strabo, says forty thousand men worked in them. Notice the frankness: the writer says that Rome fought for the mines, and admires its patience in getting them (8:4).

a: Perseus king of the Kittim
p: An old name for people of the west: here the Macedonians.
b: Kittim were first the people of Kition on Cyprus (Genesis 10:4), then westerners in general. 1 Maccabees calls Alexander's Macedon "the land of Kittim" (1:1), so Perseus, last king of Macedon, is "king of the Kittim". Philip V lost to Rome at Cynoscephalae (197 BC); his son Perseus at Pydna (168 BC). In Daniel 11:30 the "ships of Kittim" that stop Antiochus are Roman (the Greek of Daniel there says "Romans"), and in the Dead Sea Scrolls "the Kittim" are the Romans.

a: Antiochus the Great, king of Asia
p: Antiochus III, father of Antiochus IV and grandfather of the later kings, crushed by Rome in 190 BC.
b: Antiochus III, father of Antiochus IV, invaded Greece and was beaten by Rome at Thermopylae (191 BC) and Magnesia (190 or 189 BC). The treaty of Apamea (188 BC) took his lands west of the Taurus mountains, imposed a huge payment and hostages, and forbade him elephants. Daniel 11:18–19 seems to describe the same defeat: "a commander will put an end to his insolence".

a: They took him alive
t: An error: Antiochus was not captured
p: Rome never captured Antiochus III; his son was taken as a hostage instead.
b: Antiochus III fled from Magnesia and made peace; he was never taken alive. The writer may be confusing him with his son, the future Antiochus IV, who went to Rome as a hostage under the peace terms (1:10). Errors like this, in a report Judas "heard", fit the book's frame: it tells what Judea knew of Rome, at a distance (8:1).

a: a set portion
p: The Greek word is obscure: a fixed payment, a settlement, or a ceded territory.
b: Diastolē means a "separation" or "distinction", and in this verse probably something fixed by the terms of peace. The KJV has "that which was agreed upon". Some take it as land to be handed over, linking it with the provinces of 8:8; others as a fixed sum. The treaty of Apamea (188 BC) did both: it took Asia Minor west of the Taurus and set a large indemnity. The Plain keeps the vague sense.

a: the country of India, Media and Lydia
p: Rome never held India or Media; the names are probably garbled.
b: At Apamea Rome took Asia Minor west of the Taurus, and gave much of it to its ally King Eumenes II of Pergamum. Lydia fits; India and Media do not. Many scholars think the Hebrew or the Greek once read "Ionia" and "Mysia", regions Eumenes did receive, and that copyists turned them into better-known names. All Swete's manuscripts, the Latin and the KJV have India and Media, so the Plain keeps them.
orig: χώραν τὴν Ἰνδικὴν καὶ Μηδίαν καὶ Λυδίαν

a: The Greeks had planned to come and destroy them
p: It sounds like Rome's war with the Achaean League, which ended with Corinth burned in 146 BC, after Judas's death.
b: "A single general" defeated the Greeks, enslaved women and children and tore down their walls (8:10). That best fits 146 BC, when Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth and enslaved its people. If so, the writer has put into Judas's hearing a war that happened fourteen years after his death (160 BC), which shows that he wrote later and was summing up Rome's record. Others point to Rome's earlier war with the Aetolian League (191–189 BC).

a: But with their friends and with those who relied on them, they kept up friendship
p: After chapter 7's oath-breakers, the writer prizes a power that keeps its word.
b: The chapter sets Rome against the Seleucids: they broke oaths (6:62; 7:18), Rome keeps faith with its friends. That is what Judas wants. Historians are less sure Rome deserved it: Gruen argues that Rome made such pacts freely because they cost nothing, and it did nothing when Demetrius killed Judas soon after (9:1–18). Readers in Jesus' day, under Roman rule, could hardly have written this chapter; the Psalms of Solomon (about 50 BC) curse Pompey as a sinner who defiled Jerusalem.

a: Whomever they wished to help and to make king, became king
p: The Seleucids knew it well: Rome had stopped Antiochus IV in Egypt with a word.
b: In 168 BC a Roman envoy, Popilius Laenas, met Antiochus IV outside Alexandria, drew a circle around him in the sand, and told him to answer before stepping out of it whether he would leave Egypt. Antiochus left (Polybius 29.27). Daniel 11:30 seems to describe the same moment: "ships of Kittim will come against him, and he will lose heart". Rome also held Demetrius as a hostage and had refused to make him king (7:1).

a: none of them wore a crown or dressed in purple
p: The writer admires a state without royal crowns, though his own heroes later wore purple.
b: Rome was a republic; its magistrates wore a purple-bordered toga, but no one wore a crown, and the title "king" was hated. The Seleucid kings, by contrast, wore the diadem and sent purple robes as honors. The irony is that the Hasmoneans themselves accepted the purple (10:20, 62; 14:43–44) and, from about 104 BC, called themselves kings. A century after this book, Rome had an emperor, and soldiers mocked Jesus with a purple robe and a crown of thorns (Mark 15:17).

a: three hundred twenty men met there in council
p: The Senate had about three hundred members and did not meet every day.
b: The bouleutērion is the Senate house, the Curia. In this period the Senate had about 300 members; "320" may be a slip or include other officials. It met when called, not daily. The writer's picture is idealized but not far off: Rome was governed by a council of its leading men.

a: Every year they entrusted their rule to one man
p: Rome elected two consuls each year; the writer knows only one.
b: Rome's chief magistrates were the two consuls, elected yearly and each able to block the other. The writer may have known only of the consul who presided, or who wrote letters in Rome's name (15:16 names one consul, Lucius). "No envy or rivalry" was untrue even then, and became bitterly untrue in the civil wars that began with the Gracchi (133 BC) and ended with the Caesars. Some take this as a sign that the book was written before those wars were widely known.

a: Eupolemus son of John son of Accos
p: A priest of the house of Hakkoz, probably the Jewish historian Eupolemus.
b: Accos is the priestly family of Hakkoz (1 Chronicles 24:10), which once could not prove its descent (Ezra 2:61–62) but was later accepted (Nehemiah 3:4, 21). Eupolemus's father John had won privileges for the Jews from Antiochus III (2 Maccabees 4:11). Many scholars identify the envoy with Eupolemus the historian, whose Greek work on the kings of Judah survives in quotations (Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, book 9). A Jew of Jerusalem who wrote Greek history is a good choice of envoy to Rome.

a: to lift the yoke from them
p: Judas wants Rome to lift the Greek yoke. A century later Rome laid its own.
b: "Yoke" is the Hebrew Bible's picture of foreign rule (Leviticus 26:13; Jeremiah 28:2). Judas hopes Rome will free Israel from the Greek kingdom. In 63 BC Pompey entered Jerusalem and the Temple, and Judea paid tribute to Rome from then on. Later Jewish tradition remembered that Rome "kept faith with Israel" for only a time before it subjugated them (Bavli Avodah Zarah 8b–9a). The irony was not lost on readers after AD 70, when Rome burned the Temple.

a: to be enrolled as your allies and friends
p: The formula of Roman diplomacy: socii et amici.
b: "Allies and friends" (symmachoi kai philoi) translates the Latin socii et amici. Being "enrolled" means being written on Rome's official list of friends. It is the first time a Jewish state appears in Roman diplomacy; Jonathan and Simon renew the bond (12:1–4; 14:16–24; 15:15–24).
orig: γραφῆναι ἡμᾶς συμμάχους καὶ φίλους ὑμῶν

a: on bronze tablets
p: Most historians accept that a treaty was made in 161 BC, though the text has been shaped.
b: Rome kept its treaties on bronze tablets on the Capitol, and sent copies to its partners (Polybius 3.26 speaks of such tablets). Josephus gives a similar text (Antiquities 12.416–419). Older scholars sometimes doubted it, since Rome gained nothing; most today accept that the treaty is real, translated from a Latin or Greek original into the book's Hebrew and back into Greek, with its form much like other Roman treaties of the time. Gruen argues it was real but, for Rome, of little weight.

a: Good fortune to the Romans and to the nation of the Jews
p: The treaty begins with the usual wish for good fortune.
b: Kalōs genoito, "may it go well", is a standard Greek opening for a treaty or decree. Note that the Jews are "a nation" (ethnos) and later "the people" (dēmos, 8:29), the terms Rome used for a self-governing community.

a: as the occasion requires of them
p: Each side may judge when help is "required": Rome never sent an army.
b: The clause "as the occasion requires" (literally "as the time shall dictate to them") left each side free to decide when to act. In practice Rome sent letters, not soldiers (8:31–32; 15:16–21). The Jews' duties were real; Rome's were promises. Within months of the treaty Judas fell at Elasa, and Rome did nothing (9:1–18).
orig: ὡς ἂν ὁ καιρὸς ὑπογραφῇ αὐτοῖς

a: and without deceit
p: After so much Seleucid treachery, the word stands out.
b: Chapters 6–7 were full of dolos, "deceit": peaceful words "with treachery" (7:10, 27, 30). The treaty ends Rome's side with ou meta dolou, "not with deceit". The writer wants the contrast to be felt: here at last is a partner whose word holds. On whether it did, see the note at 8:25.

a: whatever they add or take away shall be binding
p: Unlike the law of Moses, which no one may add to or take from.
b: The last clause lets either party change the terms by agreement. Readers who knew Deuteronomy would notice the contrast: "Do not add anything to the word I am commanding you, and do not take anything away from it" (Deuteronomy 4:2). A human treaty is open to revision; God's covenant is not. The writer does not draw the lesson, but the echo marks the difference between the two kinds of agreement.

a: Why have you made your yoke heavy on our friends and allies the Jews?
p: Rome speaks to Demetrius in the words Israel used to Rehoboam.
b: "Your father made our yoke heavy" was Israel's complaint to Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:10; compare 1 Kings 12:4). In the Greek of 1 Maccabees, Rome uses the same picture against Demetrius. The letter claims to have been written already; the book gives no reply, and Demetrius sends Bacchides against Judas at once (9:1).

a: we will do them justice and fight you by sea and by land
p: A great power's promise. Prophets had warned against leaning on such promises.
b: Isaiah warned those who "go down to Egypt for help" and trust in horses (Isaiah 31:1), and the seer Hanani rebuked King Asa: "Because you leaned on the king of Aram and did not lean on the LORD your God" (2 Chronicles 16:7). The Psalms say, "Do not rely on nobles" (Psalm 146:3). 1 Maccabees does not criticize Judas for the treaty, and Jonathan and Simon renew it (12:1; 14:18). 2 Maccabees, by contrast, credits God alone with Nicanor's defeat (2 Maccabees 15:21–27). See the deep section on alliances.
